description.p: A question asked before there is anything to lose.

section.label: Source
section.p: The wisdom of Silenus, which has several witnesses: Aristotle's lost dialogue Eudemus, preserved in Plutarch's Consolatio ad Apollonium; Theognis, Elegies, lines 425–428, where the saying appears as a proverb (Stobaeus attributes a version to Alcidamas, and the numbering was confirmed only through a secondary page); Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus, the chorus near lines 1224–1227 (the translation consulted shows markers at 1220 and 1230 around it, so the range is plausible but was not checked line by line); and Nietzsche, Die Geburt der Tragödie (The Birth of Tragedy, 1872), section 3. A modern philosophical form is David Benatar, Better Never to Have Been (Oxford, 2006).

section.label: Argument
section.p: Midas asks the captive Silenus what is best for human beings. In Nietzsche's telling the answer is: "What is best of all is for ever beyond your reach: not to be born, not to be, to be nothing" (Haussmann translation). Second best is to die soon. Benatar gives the saying an argument. The absence of pain is good even when no one enjoys that absence, whereas the absence of pleasure is bad only if someone is deprived of it. Since the unborn lack both and nobody is deprived, non-existence has the advantage, and coming into existence is a harm.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: Silenus, old and drunken, laughs as he answers, and Midas recoils from what he hears. The laughter stands for a wisdom older than the gods of Olympus, given reluctantly and without pity. The spring and the rose garden, where Silenus was caught in one version of the story, mark the ordinary pleasures from which the question is asked. The blank margin of the etching, the paper itself, is the unborn.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A question asked before there is anything to lose. The card names the thought, which most people meet at some point, that existence was not a favour. It marks a starting premise and does not predict an outcome.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: Critics of Benatar, among them David DeGrazia and Aaron Smuts, dispute the asymmetry, and a common reply is that it is stipulated and not derived. Another reply is that goods and bads need a subject, so that "better for the unborn" has no one to whom it applies. Nietzsche reports the saying and then argues that the Greeks answered it with the Olympian gods, who made life worth living.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — The Last Messiah: the card that returns to this one. I — The Giant Deer: the biological form of the complaint. XI — The Stone: the one response that accepts being born.

description.p: An awareness greater than the situation requires.

section.label: Source
section.p: Peter Wessel Zapffe, "Den sidste Messias" ("The Last Messiah"), Janus, 1933, a short version of the book Om det tragiske (1941); the dates are taken from the research note and were not rechecked. The English text consulted is the Philosophy Now translation (issue 45).

section.label: Argument
section.p: Zapffe describes human consciousness as a biological paradox: an organ developed beyond the needs of survival, which turns against its bearer. He compares it to the antlers of a deer that grew too heavy to carry. A creature that sees its own mortality, the indifference of the world and the suffering in it lives in what he calls cosmic panic. The essay opens with a parable of the first man who wakes to this understanding at a waterhole.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A single deer stands in a bare winter forest, its head bowed under antlers wider than its body. The antlers stand for an endowment that has outgrown its use and become a burden. The empty forest shows a creature alone with its excess. The species was extinct long before Zapffe wrote, which suits an image of a line that ends.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: An awareness greater than the situation requires: a person who thinks more than the day demands, or who finds ordinary life harder because he sees too much of it. The card names the cost of insight and invites a question about what to do with it.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: The antler story is an analogy and not an argument, and the zoology was not checked here. A more serious objection is that consciousness is also the source of the values by which suffering is judged bad; a verdict delivered by the faculty the argument condemns carries the same doubt. Camus, who did not read Zapffe, accepts a similar diagnosis of the gap between human demands and the silence of the world and declines the conclusion.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — The Last Messiah: the essay's own ending and the card that completes this one. X — The Insomniac: lucidity as the same excess felt nightly. 0 — The Unborn: the state before the burden.

description.p: Satisfaction pursued in the immediate, achieved, and not felt.

section.label: Source
section.p: Eduard von Hartmann, Philosophie des Unbewussten (Philosophy of the Unconscious, 1869), as summarised in the excerpt on the Utah Ethics of Suicide site, which uses William Chatterton Coupland's 1893 translation. The research note records that Britannica describes a different triad, about the Unconscious itself; that was not examined here.

section.label: Argument
section.p: Hartmann holds that humanity passes through three stages of illusion, each ending in disappointment. In the first, happiness is sought in earthly life in the present. He associates the stage with antiquity and with childhood. Experience then shows that the goods of this life do not deliver the happiness they promise: pleasures are brief and mixed with pain, and desire renews itself as it is satisfied.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: Children play in a classical garden, the age and the era Hartmann pairs with the first stage. The hoop and the wreath stand for pleasure in the present. A soap bubble drifts above them, the homo bulla of vanitas painting, and a hairline crack runs through the fountain basin: the signs of fragility are small and easy to miss, as they are in the stage itself.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Satisfaction pursued in the immediate: money, pleasure, comfort, reputation. The card describes the point at which the pursuit has been achieved and the contentment has not arrived, or has arrived and gone. It does not say that pleasure is worthless.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: Epicurus and Aristotle held that a moderate happiness in this life is available and sufficient, so that the failure of excess does not show the failure of the whole. Hartmann's claim that experience proves the illusion is itself an empirical claim, and it is contested by the evidence that most people report being satisfied with their lives.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the next stage, once this world is given up. V — Vanity: the same observation made by Ecclesiastes two millennia earlier. VI — The Pendulum: Schopenhauer's account of why satisfaction fails.

description.p: Deferred fulfilment: effort now, to be repaid elsewhere.

section.label: Source
section.p: Eduard von Hartmann, Philosophie des Unbewussten (1869), stage two of the three illusions, via the Utah excerpt (Coupland translation, 1893).

section.label: Argument
section.p: After the first illusion fails, happiness is relocated to a transcendent life after death. Hartmann associates this stage with the Middle Ages and with youth. The stage meets its own disappointment: the hope of a heaven devalues the present world, and with the decline of belief the hope loses its force. In Hartmann's account it is exhausted historically, as faith recedes, and in the individual, as the believer ages.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: Pilgrims with staffs and scallop shells look up at a heavenly city resting on cloud. The pilgrimage stands for a life organised around a destination elsewhere. The lower walls of the city are thinning into cloud, so that sky shows through the stone: the hope remains in view while its support gives way.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Deferred fulfilment: the belief that effort, suffering or patience now will be repaid elsewhere, in a religion, a promised retirement or a future life. The card asks what is being postponed and for whom.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: The religious traditions reply that the afterlife is the ground of meaning and that its loss is the problem, which would make the pessimist's argument a symptom and not a finding. Nietzsche made the reverse charge, that the other-worldly hope slanders the present life. A narrower objection is that Hartmann treats the stage as a historical fact about what people believe, which says nothing on whether the belief is true.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the stage that this one replaces. IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the hope transferred to the future of the world. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: Schopenhauer's renunciation, which Hartmann judged a private escape.

description.p: Faith in a future that will justify the present.

section.label: Source
section.p: Eduard von Hartmann, Philosophie des Unbewussten (1869), stage three, via the Utah excerpt (Coupland translation, 1893).

section.label: Argument
section.p: In the third stage happiness is placed in the future development of the world: in science, politics and the improvement of the species. Hartmann associates it with modern times and with adulthood. He expects it to fail in turn, because additional means to satisfaction create additional wants. Having dismissed all three, he draws a conclusion that differs from Schopenhauer's. He rejects individual suicide as selfish and pointless, since the world-will would continue in other forms. He proposes instead that the world-process could end only if humanity as a whole came to will its cessation, a "cosmic-universal negation of will as the act that forms the end of the process" (Coupland).

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A procession in 19th-century dress walks toward a horizon of chimneys and railway lines, led by a man with a blank pennant. The road and the rails converge on a destination that grows fainter as it nears. The blank pennant is a cause with no stated content.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Faith in a future that will justify the present: the plan, the cause, the career that ends in a better life. The card questions whether a goal that always lies ahead can supply the happiness that is missing now.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: Measures of health, literacy and material welfare have improved over the long run, and a piecemeal improvement does not require a final state. There is also an internal objection: Hartmann's own endpoint, a collective act that ends the world-process, is a progress narrative with a teleology of its own. Dienstag, who studies the pessimists as a tradition, argues that progress is not a lasting feature of history, which supports Hartmann on the point.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the hope that progress replaced. XV — The Last Messiah: a different collective ending, by refusal and not by willing. XIII — The Broom: a response that gives up progress and keeps solidarity.

description.p: Labour whose point has gone, or a success that arrives without satisfaction.

section.label: Source
section.p: Ecclesiastes (Qohelet), chapters 1–3. The book was composed between about 450 and 180 BCE, and scholars divide between the Persian and the Hellenistic period. The Vulgate's vanitas vanitatum (1:2) gave the vanitas still life its name.

section.label: Argument
section.p: The Hebrew hevel means vapour or breath and is rendered "vanity", "futility" or "meaningless". The Preacher examines wisdom, wealth, pleasure and labour "under the sun", a phrase that recurs twenty-nine times, and finds each transient. In the King James translation: "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity." He asks what profit a man has from his toil (1:3). Chapter 3 pairs a time to be born with a time to die, and a time to weep with a time to laugh, in a cycle that adds up to no gain.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A skull, an hourglass and a snuffed candle lie among tools of labour: spade, hammer, compasses and a closed ledger. The skull and hourglass mark mortality and time, the candle a life put out, and the tools the toil from which no profit remains. An open window shows a bright sun, the "under the sun" of the Preacher, which shines on all of it alike.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Labour whose point has gone, or a success that arrives without satisfaction. The card names the afternoon when the work still has to be done and the question of its worth has been asked.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: The book contradicts its own gloom. The Preacher also advises enjoyment of food, work and companionship as gifts, and the epilogue (12:13) counsels fear of God and keeping the commandments, though many modern commentators think the epilogue was added to make the book orthodox. Whether Ecclesiastes is a pessimist text or a text about how to live with transience is disputed.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the same finding stated as a stage in an argument. VI — The Pendulum: Schopenhauer's explanation of the cycle. XI — The Stone: a later image of labour without gain, answered differently.

description.p: The swing between pressure and flatness, which a change of circumstance will not stop.

section.label: Source
section.p: Arthur Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (The World as Will and Representation, 1818, enlarged 1844), volume I, §57. The section number was confirmed in the Haldane–Kemp translation on Project Gutenberg.

section.label: Argument
section.p: Schopenhauer holds that willing arises from want, and that want is suffering. When a desire is satisfied the pleasure is only the removal of a lack. With the lack gone, emptiness and boredom follow, and a new want soon appears. In the Haldane–Kemp translation: "Thus its life swings like a pendulum backwards and forwards between pain and ennui." The theory treats pleasure as negative, a relief from pain, and pain as positive.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A great pendulum hangs over a bare plain. At one end of its swing a figure is doubled over in pain; at the other a man yawns on a stone with a closed book at his feet. The pendulum stands for the will's motion between want and its satisfaction, and the two figures for the two states it passes through. The symmetry of the scene shows that neither end is a resting place.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The oscillation between pressure and flatness: a busy period followed by a restless one, a goal reached followed by a drift. The card does not condemn either state. It names the pattern and suggests that changing the circumstances will not stop the swing.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: Nietzsche rejected the premise that life is basically a matter of suffering, and the claim that pleasure is merely negative is the weakest point of the argument. Experiences of absorbed activity do not fit the picture, since they involve neither a prior want nor a subsequent emptiness. Schopenhauer's own exceptions, aesthetic contemplation and compassion, concede that the pendulum can be stopped.

section.label: Links
section.p: XIV — The Stilled Wheel: Schopenhauer's answer, the moment when the swing stops. II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the hope the pendulum defeats. X — The Insomniac: boredom as a waking state.

description.p: A complaint addressed to a world that does not listen.

section.label: Source
section.p: Giacomo Leopardi, "Dialogo della Natura e di un Islandese" (Dialogue between Nature and an Icelander), in the Operette morali, written in 1824. The English text consulted is Charles Edwardes, Essays and Dialogues of Giacomo Leopardi (1882), on Project Gutenberg.

section.label: Argument
section.p: An Icelander who has fled Nature across the world meets her in inner Africa, a giantess seated against a mountain. He complains that she has caused his suffering. She replies that the world was not made for human beings: "What I do is in no sense done for your enjoyment or benefit, as you seem to think" (Edwardes). She adds that creation and destruction are one process and that she would not notice the loss of the human race. Critics read the dialogue as Leopardi's turn from a historical pessimism, which blames civilisation, to a cosmic one, which blames nature.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A small traveller in a heavy northern coat stands before a colossal woman seated with her back against a mountain, her face between beautiful and terrible, as Leopardi describes her. The scale is the argument: the traveller's grievance is addressed to something that does not register him. The barren plain is the interior of Africa where he finds her, at the far end of his flight.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A complaint addressed to a world that does not listen. The card names the moment of finding that illness, accident or loss has no author who could answer for it, and that the grievance has no one to receive it.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: A nature that is indifferent cannot be accused of cruelty, and the Icelander's protest presumes the purposes it denies. A theist would say the dialogue personifies a mechanism and then blames the person it has invented. The dialogue anticipates this by making Nature a character who is amused by the question.

section.label: Links
section.p: XIII — The Broom: Leopardi's later poem, which keeps this nature and adds a human answer. I — The Giant Deer: the same indifference seen from the biology of the mind. IX — The Shattered God: a metaphysics that gives the indifference an origin.

description.p: A question of closeness: how near to stand to others.

section.label: Source
section.p: Arthur Schopenhauer, Parerga und Paralipomena (1851), volume II. One secondary source gives chapter XXXI, §396; another places the passage in a chapter of psychological observations, and the German text was not consulted, so the section number is unconfirmed. The English text used is the parable "A Few Parables" in T. Bailey Saunders's Studies in Pessimism (Project Gutenberg), where the translator is not named in the part of the page that was fetched.

section.label: Argument
section.p: On a cold day porcupines huddle together for warmth and prick one another with their quills, so they move apart, and the cold drives them back. They repeat this until they find a distance at which they can bear each other. In the Saunders translation, "the need of society drives the human porcupines together, only to be mutually repelled." Schopenhauer concludes that good manners and courtesy are the moderate distance found by experience. Freud quoted the parable in a footnote in 1921.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: Porcupines sit on snow at a settled distance from one another, and one pair, still too close, is flinching apart. The cold stands for the need of company, the quills for the faults that make company painful, and the gaps for the courtesy that Schopenhauer says is learned from both.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A question of closeness: how near to stand to a friend, a family, a colleague. The card does not advise withdrawal. It describes a relationship at which the warmth is real and the distance has been worked out.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: The parable ends in an equilibrium, which is a less pessimistic result than the rest of the tradition would predict. Attachment research and Aristotle's account of friendship suggest that intimacy changes the quills: people who know each other well hurt each other less, not more. The image also assumes a fixed physical nature in both parties.

section.label: Links
section.p: XII — Compassion: the capacity that, in Schopenhauer, allows closeness without injury. X — The Insomniac: the isolated end of the range. XIII — The Broom: solidarity as the case in which the cold forces cooperation.

description.p: Living among the remains of something that has ended.

section.label: Source
section.p: Philipp Mainländer, Die Philosophie der Erlösung (The Philosophy of Redemption), volume I, 1876; volume II, 1886. Mainländer was born in 1841 and died in 1876, the day after the first volume was published. No scholarly encyclopedia entry was found, and the summary below rests on Wikipedia and on a recent journal article by A. V. Popkov, "The Will to Die as a Basic Metaphysical Principle", which was seen only as a search result. No public-domain English translation was located, so the card carries no quotation.

section.label: Argument
section.p: Mainländer begins from an original unity, God, who wished for non-existence and could reach it only by dissolving into a world of many things. The world is the remains of that act: matter, life and the stars are God's fragments, driven by a will to die that underlies the apparent will to live. History tends to nothingness. Unlike Schopenhauer, Mainländer takes the will as plural, with many finite wills and not one, and holds that death brings absolute nothingness. His ethics follows from the metaphysics, and he argued that enlightened self-interest leads toward asceticism and, as a social aim, toward the gradual decline of the species.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A vast pale sphere breaks along fine cracks, and its fragments drift outward, becoming stars, stones, a tree, a fish, a bird and a small walking figure. The sphere is featureless because Mainländer's original unity cannot be pictured. The things of the world appear as its remains, and their dispersal as the slow course of its dying.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A sense that the parts of one's world are remains of something that has ended: a family, an institution, a belief. The card names the condition of living among fragments and invites the question of what the whole was.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: The system is a speculative cosmology without independent evidence, and it asserts a divine act that has no witness. Schopenhauer's single will was criticised for its remoteness from experience, and Mainländer's plurality does not escape the charge. Nietzsche, in The Gay Science §357, dismissed Mainländer in a single scornful phrase.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — Nature and the Icelander: an indifferent nature, here given a history. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: Schopenhauer's denial of the will, which Mainländer reinterprets. XV — The Last Messiah: another proposal for an orderly end.

description.p: Lucidity without relief, to be endured and put to use.

section.label: Source
section.p: Emil Cioran, Pe culmile disperării (On the Heights of Despair, 1934, written in Romanian); Précis de décomposition (A Short History of Decay, Gallimard, 1949); De l'inconvénient d'être né (The Trouble with Being Born, Gallimard, 1973). Cioran suffered from insomnia from the age of twenty for the rest of his life and wrote that his first book grew out of a sleepless night. He died in Paris in 1995. These details come from a single encyclopedia page. No public-domain translation exists, and the card has no quotation.

section.label: Argument
section.p: Cioran writes in aphorisms and does not build an argument. His theme is lucidity: the wakeful mind sees what sleep and habit hide, and cannot stop seeing it. Being born is an inconvenience, a condition imposed on a person that he spends his life accommodating. On suicide, Cioran was drawn to the idea and regarded it as a consolation that helped him to keep living; he did not recommend the act. The card draws on the insomnia and the lucidity, and not on that thought.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A man sits awake at an open window at night with a lamp beside him, above a city that sleeps. The lamp stands for lucidity, which keeps him company and keeps him awake. The image inverts Goya's Capricho 43, in which reason sleeps and the creatures of the night are awake; here the world sleeps and one mind does not.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A period of wakefulness in which one sees clearly and without relief: a night of worry, a long illness, an obsession with a question. The card names lucidity as a condition that has to be endured and that the sufferer can learn to use.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: A critic can ask whether wakefulness gives accurate sight or a distortion of its own, because the exhausted mind is a poor judge of the value of life. Aphorism also leaves its claims unargued, and Dienstag counts Cioran among the existential pessimists who write for the edification of the reader. Camus offered the opposite resolution: lucidity as the ground of a lived happiness.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — The Giant Deer: the same excess of mind, now in the night. VI — The Pendulum: the boredom that fills the hours. XI — The Stone: the response of a lucid person who decides to carry on.

description.p: Persistence in work without a promise of result.

section.label: Source
section.p: Albert Camus, Le Mythe de Sisyphe (The Myth of Sisyphus), written in 1941 and published in 1942. The summary rests on the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Camus, and no public-domain translation exists, so the card has no quotation.

section.label: Argument
section.p: The absurd arises from the gap between the human demand for meaning and the silence of the world. Camus opens by calling suicide the one serious philosophical problem, since it asks whether life is worth living. He rejects it, and he rejects the two other exits from the absurd, hope in another world and a great cause. He recommends lucid revolt: to live without consolation and without reconciling oneself. Sisyphus, condemned to push a stone that rolls back, is the model. In the descent, when he knows his situation fully, he is superior to his fate. Camus concludes that one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: Sisyphus walks down the mountain with a steady step, and the boulder lies at rest at its foot. Camus singles out this descent, when Sisyphus returns to his task knowing it fully. The stone stands for a labour without result, and the empty hands for the pause in which the labour can be faced.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Persistence in work without a promise of result. The card names the disposition of someone who continues with a task that is neither finished nor justified, and the possibility that the continuing is its own answer.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: The Stanford entry notes a shift from scepticism to a normative stance, which it calls a sleight of hand. On Zapffe's terms, revolt could be read as one of the anchoring mechanisms, a way of fixing attention on a task so as to avoid the panic, which would make the happy Sisyphus another of the evasions. Schopenhauer would say that the stone is the will itself, and that carrying it gladly misunderstands the problem.

section.label: Links
section.p: 0 — The Unborn: the premise Camus accepts without the conclusion. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: renunciation as the opposite answer. VI — The Pendulum: the same repeated cycle, met with a different attitude.

description.p: Helping someone because they suffer, with no calculation of return.

section.label: Source
section.p: Arthur Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung, volume I, book IV, §§66–69; and Über die Grundlage der Moral (On the Basis of Morality, 1840). In the Haldane–Kemp translation of the first work, Mitleid is rendered "sympathy". The three incentives of the second work, egoism, malice and compassion, were confirmed only through secondary summaries, which cite §16 for the discussion. The Payne translation was not consulted.

section.label: Argument
section.p: Schopenhauer holds that actions arise from three fundamental incentives: egoism, which seeks one's own good; malice, which seeks another's harm; and compassion, which seeks another's good for its own sake. Only compassion gives an action moral worth. It rests on a recognition that the suffering of another is, at the level of the will, one's own. In the Haldane–Kemp translation: "all true and pure love is sympathy, and all love which is not sympathy is selfishness." Schopenhauer argues against suicide on the same ground: in §69 he writes that it is "a phenomenon of strong assertion of will", because the person who ends his life rejects the conditions of his life and not the will to live.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A woman kneels beside a stranger lying by the road, her hand on his shoulder, while a boy brings water to a dog with a bandaged leg. The stranger is unknown to her, which marks compassion as a response to suffering as such, without a tie of kin. The dog follows Schopenhauer's insistence that compassion extends to animals.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The pull toward helping someone because they suffer, with no calculation of return. The card names a moral disposition and the cost of keeping it, which is that the helper takes on part of the pain.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: Nietzsche treated pity as a weakness that multiplies suffering by sharing it. A second objection comes from within the system: if life is on the whole an evil, compassion that preserves and comforts the sufferer prolongs the evil, and Schopenhauer's reply is that it is a step toward renunciation. Hartmann objected that individual renunciation is a private escape that leaves the world-process untouched.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Porcupines: the distance that compassion crosses. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: the next step in Schopenhauer's sequence. XIII — The Broom: compassion made collective.

description.p: Dignity in a precarious place, and joining with others in it.

section.label: Source
section.p: Giacomo Leopardi, "La ginestra, o il fiore del deserto" ("The Broom, or the Flower of the Desert", 1836), his last major poem. Only secondary summaries were consulted, from Italian study sites and an article in the journal Between (2015). The primary text and the line numbers were not checked, and the reference to the "social chain" at line 149 comes from the Between article.

section.label: Argument
section.p: The poem is set on the slope of Vesuvius, where a broom grows on the hardened lava. The poet addresses a century that believes in progress and invites its readers to the mountain, where the power of nature and the smallness of humanity are visible. The broom accepts its situation without denial and without pride. Against a nature that harms all people alike, Leopardi proposes a social catena, a social chain: a union of human beings who recognise a common enemy and give each other help. Solidarity is the reasoned response to pessimism.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: Broom flowers on black lava, with Vesuvius smoking above and a ruined Roman town below. The broom stands for a life that grows where it has been placed, without denying the danger or claiming to defeat it. The buried town shows what the mountain has already done, and no people are drawn: the human chain the poem calls for is left to the reader.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Dignity in a precarious place and the decision to join with others in it. The card names the stance of someone who has seen the situation clearly and works with others on the ground that remains.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: A pessimist can ask what grounds the solidarity. If existence is on the whole an evil, the reason to sustain a human chain against nature is unclear, and Zapffe would count the appeal as an anchoring mechanism. A different objection is that the poem's tone toward the optimism of its time is sarcastic, which sits oddly with its own constructive proposal. The secondary sources disagree on how far the poem is a political programme.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — Nature and the Icelander: the indifferent nature that the broom endures. XII — Compassion: the personal disposition from which the chain is made. IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the faith the poem opposes.

description.p: A pause in the cycle of wanting.

section.label: Source
section.p: Arthur Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung, volume I: §38, on aesthetic contemplation, and §68, on asceticism and the denial of the will. Both sections were confirmed in the Haldane–Kemp translation and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Schopenhauer.

section.label: Argument
section.p: In aesthetic contemplation the knower becomes a pure, will-less subject for a time, and the striving that drives the pendulum is suspended. In the Haldane–Kemp translation: "the wheel of Ixion stands still." The state is temporary. The lasting form is the denial of the will in §68: the saint, seeing through the illusion of separate individuals, ceases to will, accepts poverty and chastity, and reaches a calm that Schopenhauer describes as a relative nothing, the absence of the will and not its opposite. He distinguishes this sharply from suicide, which he regards as an affirmation of the will (§69).

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A large spoked wheel stands motionless in long grass, ivy over its rim, and a figure sits beside it facing away, toward a wide valley. The wheel is Ixion's, empty and at rest, as in Schopenhauer's image of aesthetic contemplation. The ivy shows that it has been still for some time. The seated figure looks at the view without wanting anything from it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A pause in the cycle of wanting, in music, a landscape or a piece of work. The card names relief that comes from attention and not from acquisition, and notes that it ends.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: Nietzsche rejected the denial of the will as hostility to life and held that the will to power affirms it. Hartmann objected that the ascetic seeks a private escape and leaves the world-process untouched. There is also a doubt about the argument: if the saint's calm is a relative nothing, the description has little content, and Schopenhauer admits that it cannot be put in words.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — The Pendulum: the swing that is stilled. XII — Compassion: the step before it in Schopenhauer's sequence. XI — The Stone: the opposite answer, which keeps willing.

description.p: The conclusion of a long argument, and the question of whether to follow it.

section.label: Source
section.p: Peter Wessel Zapffe, "Den sidste Messias", Janus, 1933, in the Philosophy Now translation (issue 45). The essay sets out four mechanisms for damping consciousness and closes with the Messiah's message.

section.label: Argument
section.p: People survive, in Zapffe's account, by limiting what enters consciousness. Isolation shuts out disturbing thought. Anchoring fixes the flow of experience to points such as God, the nation or the family. Distraction fills attention. Sublimation turns pain into art, and Zapffe treats it as the rarest. After a series of failed saviours there comes a last Messiah, who sees the human condition fully. The Philosophy Now translation gives his message as: "Know yourselves – be infertile and let the earth be silent after ye." The Messiah descends from the first man at the waterhole. Zapffe presents this as a vision and not as a plan.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: A lone man on a rise speaks to a crowd, most of whom have turned their backs and are walking away. Beyond them lies an empty, quiet landscape under a wide sky: the silent earth of his message. The crowd's turning shows the reception Zapffe predicts; in the essay they then turn on him, which the card leaves undrawn.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The conclusion of a long argument, and the question of whether one is willing to follow it. The card names the extreme end of the tradition and returns the reader to the first card.

section.label: Counterweight
section.p: Camus holds that the absurd is to be lived and that the correct response to a meaningless world is revolt and not extinction. Antinatalist arguments of this kind depend on contested premises, like Benatar's asymmetry. Hartmann, who also imagined a collective end of the world-process, saw that it would need nearly universal agreement among people who could communicate with one another, which he did not expect soon. Zapffe's own essay, which belongs to the rare mechanism of sublimation, may be read as an instance of what it describes.

section.label: Links
section.p: 0 — The Unborn: the card to which it leads. I — The Giant Deer: where the essay begins. IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: Hartmann's collective alternative, by willing and not by refusal.

description.p: A thought has been set aside before it was finished.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The truth of the Giant Deer is that awareness exceeds what the day requires. Isolation meets it by dismissing the surplus as it arises: a thought at the edge of attention is labelled overthinking and put down. The habit is taught early and is usually kind.

section.label: Image
section.p: A woman at a kitchen table pauses with a cup half raised. Her free hand lays a lid over a glass jar in which a small antlered shadow presses against the glass. The window behind her is dark.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The first small act of exclusion: a thought judged unhelpful and sent away.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A thought has been set aside before it was finished. The card asks what it was going to say, and can mark either a sound sense of proportion or the start of a long habit.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A mind that followed every implication would not get through breakfast. Zapffe holds that the surplus of consciousness must be damped for a person to function, and isolation is the cheapest means, since it needs no belief and no occupation.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — The Giant Deer: the excess being set aside. X — The Insomniac: the hour at which the setting aside fails.

description.p: An enjoyment is being shielded from scrutiny.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The First Illusion holds that happiness is to be had here and now. When a good moment shows its thinness, a dinner already ending or a holiday already half spent, isolation removes the observation. The guest declines to notice that the pleasure is fading and attends to the next dish.

section.label: Image
section.p: A long banquet table under lanterns, the guests in profile and in high spirits. One diner at the end looks into his glass, where the candle flames are shrinking. A servant behind him lifts a cloth over the dessert.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The refusal to inspect a pleasure while it lasts.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: An enjoyment is being shielded from scrutiny. The card suggests that scrutiny would have found something real, and that skipping it is a choice.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Pleasure examined too closely seldom survives the examination, and few people regret leaving it for later. A guest who audits every dinner has lost the means of enjoying one, and Zapffe would count the looking away as what the species has always done.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the hope whose weak point is left alone. V — Vanity: the Preacher takes the opposite course and looks.

description.p: A consoling phrase is doing the work of silence.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Second Illusion places fulfilment after death. In practice the thought of death is fenced off, and a formula of consolation closes the subject. At the graveside someone says that the dead are at peace, and the talk turns to lunch.

section.label: Image
section.p: Mourners in dark coats stand in rows at a cemetery. A priest raises a hand to the sky, and the people nearest the grave watch his hand and not the hole. A child at the edge has been turned to face the road.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: A hope used as a door shut on a question.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A consoling phrase is doing the work of silence. The card does not doubt the comfort. It asks whether the comfort was meant to end the thought or to accompany it.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Grief is borne better in company and ritual than in analysis, and the phrases that close a subject also let people stand together at the worst hour. A funeral is where looking is shared out.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the hope that supplies the formula. 0 — The Unborn: the question before life, fenced off as firmly.

description.p: Information is being sorted by whether it can be borne.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Third Illusion hopes that the world will improve and justify what it costs. Isolation keeps the hope intact by controlling intake: the report of a failed programme is passed over, and the report of a successful one is read twice.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man in a waistcoat sits among stacks of newspapers and cuts out columns with scissors. The cuttings fall into a basket, and the pages he keeps are pinned in neat rows. Through the open door a railway cutting runs toward a smoking horizon.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Selective reading: a faith kept by filtering what reaches it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Information is being sorted by whether it can be borne. The card asks what has been cut out, and whether the view that remains is sound or only comfortable.

section.label: Defence
section.p: No one can carry all the world's news, and a person who tried would be of use to nobody. The filter protects the energy for work that may do some good. Zapffe describes it as one of the means by which the species continues.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the hope the filter keeps alive. XIII — The Broom: the poem that looks at the mountain.

description.p: A question about the point of the work is being deferred.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Vanity is the finding that labour yields no lasting profit. Isolation keeps the finding out of working hours by treating the question of purpose as one for another occasion. It is entered in the calendar for a quieter month and not reached.

section.label: Image
section.p: A clerk at a high desk writes steadily in an open ledger. In the margin a small skull has been inked and half scratched out. On a shelf behind him a row of hourglasses is turned to face the wall.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The postponement of the question of worth.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A question about the point of the work is being deferred. The card notes that the deferral has a date, and that the date has passed more than once.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Most work is done well by people who have not settled its ultimate point, and some would not be done if they had to. Setting the question aside lets the task go forward. The Preacher himself advises enjoying toil as a gift, and Zapffe treats such suspension as ordinary practice.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Vanity: the question put off. VI — The Pendulum: the flat hours the question would otherwise fill.

description.p: A recurring flatness has been given a harmless name.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Pendulum swings between pain and boredom. The flat end of the swing, a Sunday evening or the hour after a goal is reached, is felt and then renamed. It is called tiredness or a passing mood, so that it is never taken as information about the arrangement of life.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man in an armchair at dusk, his coat still on, watches a clock on the mantel whose pendulum is hidden behind a small curtain. A tray of tea has gone cold at his elbow.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The renaming of a mood so that it need not be examined.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A recurring flatness has been given a harmless name. The name may be accurate; the card suggests testing it once.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Moods pass, and many described as emptiness are fatigue that sleep will correct. A person who read each dip as a verdict on existence would be exhausted by his own attention. Zapffe's mechanisms let a creature go on without reading each swing as a message.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — The Pendulum: the swing whose far end is renamed. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: the pause that comes from attending, where this card flinches.

description.p: A loss has no author, and attention has moved elsewhere.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Leopardi's Nature owes human beings nothing and does not notice their loss. Isolation keeps the fact at a distance by reading accident as a story: an illness or storm is given a cause, a lesson or a villain, and where none can be found the account is not asked for.

section.label: Image
section.p: A family sits at a lamplit supper while a storm wrecks the shore beyond the window. The mother draws the curtain with one hand and serves the soup with the other. Outside, a giantess, hardly more than a drift of cloud, turns away.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The habit of not dwelling on what cannot be addressed.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A loss has no author, and attention has moved elsewhere. The card asks whether the elsewhere is a rest or an avoidance.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A grievance with no one to receive it can occupy a whole life. Turning from it lets a household eat, sleep and mend what can be mended. Zapffe counts such turning as part of how people stay alive in a world that does not answer.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — Nature and the Icelander: the silence being turned from. XII — Compassion: the opposite movement, toward another's suffering.

description.p: A subject between two people is by tacit consent not raised.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Porcupines learn a bearable distance. Isolation fixes it by agreement not to speak of what pricks: two relatives keep to the weather, and the unspoken quarrel stays in a closed room of the house.

section.label: Image
section.p: Two people sit at either end of a long sofa, each reading, with a low table between them carrying a lamp and a covered dish. A door at the back of the room stands ajar on darkness. Neither looks toward it.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The silence kept between people for the sake of peace.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A subject between two people is by tacit consent not raised. The card marks the arrangement as workable and asks how long it has been in force.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Many close relations survive because certain things are not said. Schopenhauer holds that courtesy is the distance found by experience, and a distance that lets people share a table is no small achievement. Zapffe would see the silence as a useful partition.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Porcupines: the distance being kept. XII — Compassion: what might cross it.

description.p: Something has ended, and its practical aftermath is handled with great efficiency.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Mainländer's God is gone, and the world is what remains. Isolation avoids the thought by treating the broken thing as housekeeping. A family that has come apart after a death sorts the objects, shares them out and does not discuss what the whole was.

section.label: Image
section.p: In a house being cleared, a woman wraps china in newspaper. A cracked tureen has been set aside on a chair, its pieces lying in the shape of a sphere. She wraps the plate in her hand with care and does not look at the chair.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The managing of remains in place of mourning what they were.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Something has ended, and its practical aftermath is handled with great efficiency. The efficiency is itself a response, and the card asks when the other one is due.

section.label: Defence
section.p: The practical tasks after a loss are real, and doing them is often how a person stays upright through the first weeks. The packing of china is among the oldest of Zapffe's mechanisms at work. The grief is postponed and not abolished.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — The Shattered God: the whole of which these are fragments. XI — The Stone: a way of continuing that keeps the loss in view.

description.p: A clear thought arrived at a bad time and has been discounted for that reason.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Insomniac cannot stop seeing. Isolation answers the lucid hour with dismissals: it is the coffee, the hour, the lack of sleep, and things will look different in the morning. The thought is treated as a symptom of the night.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man sits up in bed with a lamp lit, a glass of water and a closed book on the table. The grey of early morning begins at the window. On the wall the large shadow of his head leans over him, and the edge of the blanket covers it.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Lucidity treated as a condition of the hour.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A clear thought arrived at a bad time and has been discounted for that reason. The hour affects the mood and does not decide whether the thought was true.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A tired mind judges badly, and discounting the conclusions of three in the morning is usually sound practice. Zapffe describes isolation as a necessary mechanism, and its use at night is the ordinary way of getting to the day.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — The Insomniac: the lucidity being discounted. I — The Giant Deer: the excess that returns when the lamp is lit.

description.p: A matter that frightens or saddens has been put down with ease.

section.label: Age
section.p: In childhood the mechanism works almost without effort. Hartmann ties the first illusion to the early years, and Schopenhauer describes the child as living in the present, without a view of the whole. A frightening fact is dropped as quickly as it is picked up, and play closes over it.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A girl of seven sits on a garden step beside a dead bird in a shoebox. She has covered it with a leaf and is looking at a snail. Behind her a window shows an adult watching, hand on the glass, not coming out.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The natural forgetting of the young.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A matter that frightens or saddens has been put down with ease. The card marks a capacity for recovery and asks whether the thing has been set aside or not yet understood.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Children could not grow if each loss had to be taken in whole, and parents rightly protect the ease with which they turn away. Zapffe's mechanisms start here, as a mercy practised before the creature knows it is practising anything.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the garden where turning away comes easily. 0 — The Unborn: the question not yet asked.

description.p: Advice is being heard and not taken in.

section.label: Age
section.p: Schopenhauer observes that the young look to the future with expectation, and Hartmann places the second illusion in youth. The mechanism takes the form of confidence: warnings from older people are heard as a description of those people, and thoughts of failure as a lapse of nerve.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A young man in a travelling coat stands on a quay with a trunk, his back to older relatives who are speaking to him. An old woman in the group raises a hand, as if to ask a question she has decided not to put.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The refusal of counsel by those who feel they have time.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Advice is being heard and not taken in. The card marks a season of boldness and asks which part of the advice was true.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Plans of any size require some deafness to the odds. A youth who weighed all that might go wrong would not leave the quay. Zapffe treats the damping of foresight as a condition of undertaking anything.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the hope that carries the young. IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the faith that makes deafness feel like vision.

description.p: A matter of weight is being handled as logistics.

section.label: Age
section.p: Schopenhauer holds that middle life brings knowledge of how things go and a growing load of cares, and Hartmann ties the third illusion to adulthood. The mechanism becomes routine: the thought is reserved for later, the diagnosis for next month, the difficult conversation for after the holiday.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A woman in her forties stands at a kitchen counter at the end of a workday, a pile of unopened letters beside her. She reads the label of a jar with great attention. A note by the telephone on the wall has been turned face down.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Administration used as a way of not attending.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A matter of weight is being handled as logistics. The card asks which of the unopened letters it is.

section.label: Defence
section.p: The adult carries other people, and the ability to put a worry in a drawer is what lets a household function. Zapffe sees isolation as an economy of attention, and most adults practise it competently. The cost falls later, after a good deal has been bought with it.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the plan that fills the calendar. VI — The Pendulum: the evening flatness the busyness holds back.

description.p: What was put off for years is now within reach.

section.label: Age
section.p: Hartmann's three illusions leave out old age, and Schopenhauer, in his essay on the periods of life, compares the first half of life to the right side of an embroidery and the second half to the wrong side, less handsome but more instructive, because it shows how the threads are joined. Isolation takes two forms: the old habit, practised so long that it is invisible, and a release, in which the dismissals lose their force.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old man sits in a garden chair with a shawl over his knees, his eyes on a shut gate. On the table beside him lie a bundle of letters tied with string and a pair of reading glasses. One end of the string has been untied.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The end of the long deferral.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: What was put off for years is now within reach. It may be smaller than was feared, or larger, and either way it can be looked at.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A lifetime of managed attention bought a lifetime of work and affection, and there is no reason to count it a loss. If the mechanism relaxes with age, it does so after it has done its service.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — The Insomniac: the lucidity old age may allow to stay. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: the calm when wanting has eased.

description.p: A wide mind has found one thing to be.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Giant Deer names a mind larger than daily life needs. Anchoring contains it by giving the mind a single fixed point, usually an occupation or a role, so that attention returns to it whenever it begins to range. A person who answers the question of who he is with the name of his post has found a post to tie the antlers to.

section.label: Image
section.p: A stag stands in a farmyard with ribbons and paper tags wound through its antlers, the other ends knotted to a fence post. A child on tiptoe is tying on one more tag. The sky behind is empty and wide, and the ground has been trodden bare in a circle.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the first fixing of a point: the title, the trade or the creed that lets a restless mind say what it is for.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A wide mind has found one thing to be. The card marks a person who answers the large question with a small, definite one, and who is steadier for it. It asks how long the cord is.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Zapffe holds that a consciousness left to its full extent cannot keep going, and that people survive by damping it. A fixed role does this cheaply. It gives the day a shape, the self a name and the excess of thought a place to rest. Most lives that look settled owe that settlement to some such post.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — The Giant Deer: the excess that the post is meant to hold in check. X — The Insomniac: the night, when the title is put down and the excess returns.

description.p: Contentment is placed in a home and the people in it.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The First Illusion locates happiness in this life, in the present. Anchoring holds off the failure of that hope by attaching it to a person: a partner, a child, a household. If the goods of the world disappoint, the family remains, and it supplies the contentment that pleasure alone did not. Disappointment is then read as a fault in the arrangements and not in the hope.

section.label: Image
section.p: A small kitchen at evening, in the manner of Goya's domestic scenes. A family sits close around a table lit by one lamp, the figures overlapping so that no gap shows between them. Through the window behind them a crowd of strangers passes in the dark street.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names happiness lodged in other people, and the walls that a household builds around it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Contentment is placed in a home and the people in it. The card describes a settled and warm arrangement, and asks whether the warmth would last if one of its members left.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Affection is among the strongest sources of meaning that people report, and Zapffe counts the family among the sturdiest anchors for that reason. It gives purpose to effort that would otherwise seem arbitrary. Few critics of the first illusion would wish a person to lose it before something else was in place.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the hope the household shelters. VIII — The Porcupines: the distance that family life has to work out.

description.p: A hope for a later reward is kept steady by routine and community.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Second Illusion defers happiness to an afterlife. Anchoring takes the hope and builds it into a practice: a church, a calendar of observance, a community that confirms the belief by sharing it. The belief is then supported by habit and company, and it does not have to be re-examined each time doubt arises.

section.label: Image
section.p: A village congregation kneels in a stone church, in the manner of Goya's engravings of crowds. Their heads are bowed in rows, and the vault above them is painted with a sky. A single figure at the back looks up through a broken window pane at the real one.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names faith held in place by structure, and the structure that holds it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A hope for a later reward is kept steady by routine and community. The card does not ask whether the belief is true. It asks what the practice does for the person who keeps it.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Zapffe names God first among the anchors, and the choice reflects how much weight the belief has carried. It gives death a meaning, grief a limit and conduct a measure. Communities of faith also supply company, ritual and care, which do not depend on the doctrine being proved.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the hope the practice secures. XII — Compassion: the care that congregations often supply, whatever their doctrine.

description.p: A cause or an organisation gives the work a direction.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Third Illusion places happiness in the progress of the world. Anchoring attaches a person to a cause or an institution that is moving toward a goal: a party, a movement, a nation. Labour for it fills the days, and the distance still to be travelled accounts for any present dissatisfaction.

section.label: Image
section.p: A column of marchers carries banners through a town square, in the manner of Klinger's crowd scenes. Every banner has been painted with a different device, and the leaders at the front hold theirs high. A woman at the roadside holds a child up to see, and the road ahead narrows into haze.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names a loyalty to a collective project, and the energy that the project returns to its members.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A cause or an organisation gives the work a direction. The card describes the steadiness of belonging to something that is going somewhere, and asks what will remain if it arrives or fails.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Zapffe lists the nation and the cause among the anchors, and they are the ones with the widest use. Collective projects have built schools, drained marshes and ended abuses, and those who joined them were seldom troubled by cosmic panic. A person who works for something larger than himself is generally easier to live with.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the faith that the cause borrows. XIII — The Broom: a common effort that makes no promise of arrival.

description.p: Work has become the frame of a life.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Vanity finds that labour under the sun leaves no profit. Anchoring answers by making the labour a calling. Work is given a name, a ladder and a reputation, and a person measures it by position and not by what remains afterwards. The question of what the toil is for is replaced by the question of what comes next.

section.label: Image
section.p: A clerk sits at a tall desk in a room of identical desks, writing in a ledger, and a framed certificate hangs above him. Through the open door a long corridor of other offices recedes. On the windowsill a candle burns down unnoticed in the daylight.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names a career held as a fixed point, and the satisfaction of rank in a hierarchy.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Work has become the frame of a life. The card describes a person who is absorbed in a career and rewarded by it, and who would find it hard to say what the days would hold without it.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Work is among the oldest sources of structure, skill and standing, and Zapffe includes the career with the anchors for that reason. It spends the hours in a way that other people recognise. The craftsman and the official are often content, and the content is real even when the Preacher would doubt its object.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Vanity: the question the career answers by distraction from it. XI — The Stone: labour continued with the question left open.

description.p: A regular pattern keeps both restlessness and flatness at a distance.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Pendulum swings between pain and boredom. Anchoring tries to hold the swing by a fixed routine: the same hours, the same places, the same company. Routine takes out the extremes of want and of emptiness and brings the two states closer together, so that neither is felt in full.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man walks the same path along a canal at the same hour, in the manner of an etching of a town at dusk. The lamplighter, the baker and a woman at a window all appear in the same places they appeared the day before. A clock on the tower has no hands.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the steadying effect of habit, and the habits that a life is built on.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A regular pattern keeps both restlessness and flatness at a distance. The card describes a life that runs on rhythm, and asks whether the rhythm has become the purpose.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Habit relieves the mind of continual decision and spares it the work of finding something to want. Zapffe's mechanisms operate mostly in this way, quietly and without the person's attention. Much of what passes for a tranquil temperament is a well-kept routine, and the benefits are plain in the years that go by without incident.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — The Pendulum: the swing that the routine flattens. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: a pause reached by attention and not by repetition.

description.p: Attachment to a homeland or a locality makes a large and indifferent world seem familiar.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Nature does not care what happens to human beings. Anchoring keeps this out of view by attaching a person to a place and a people: a home town, a homeland, a language, a landscape that is felt to be one's own. A territory with a name and a history looks as if it had been made for those who live in it.

section.label: Image
section.p: A farmer stands at the edge of his field with a boundary stone beside him, and a flag hangs on a pole behind the barn. Beyond the fence the land continues unmarked to a range of mountains. A flock of birds crosses the line without altering course.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names belonging to a place, and the borders that declare the place to be a home.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Attachment to a homeland or a locality makes a large and indifferent world seem familiar. The card describes the comfort of belonging, and the line beyond which belonging does not extend.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A person without a place has a harder life, and Zapffe puts the nation among the anchors because it gives so many people a definite sense of where they stand. Local loyalty also produces care for land and neighbours that an abstract concern for the world seldom matches.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — Nature and the Icelander: the indifference that the border does not reach. XIII — The Broom: a bond between people that does not rest on a territory.

description.p: Convention and role settle how near people stand to one another.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Porcupines find a distance at which company is bearable. Anchoring fixes that distance by institution: marriage, the club, the office, the guild. Roles and rules decide how close people stand, and the pain of misjudging the distance is mostly avoided because the form has settled the question in advance.

section.label: Image
section.p: Guests sit at a long table, each at a marked place, and the cutlery is laid in exact rows. Between each pair of neighbours a small gap has been left, wide enough for a hand. At the head of the table a master of ceremonies holds a staff, in the manner of Goya's satirical gatherings.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the form that regulates closeness, and the relief it gives to those who follow it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Convention and role settle how near people stand to one another. The card describes a relationship that works because its terms are fixed, and asks what the terms leave unsaid.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Schopenhauer found good manners to be the distance learned from experience, and a formal arrangement preserves that knowledge. Rules spare people the injuries of working it out afresh. Many bonds that would not have survived intimacy have lasted well under a form.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Porcupines: the distance that the form fixes in advance. XII — Compassion: the response that goes beyond the places the form assigns.

description.p: A heritage or an institution is held up as the thing that makes the pieces cohere.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Shattered God shows a world of fragments with no whole behind it. Anchoring answers with a tradition, a lineage or a cause large enough to be treated as the whole: a body of belief, a family name, a heritage handed down. The fragments are read as parts of something that still holds together.

section.label: Image
section.p: An old man stands in a gallery of portraits, each of his ancestors in a gilt frame. The frames at the far end hold only cracked canvas, and he faces the nearer ones. On the floor a child assembles a broken jar from its pieces.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the effort to treat the fragments as a whole by means of a tradition.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A heritage or an institution is held up as the thing that makes the pieces cohere. The card describes loyalty to a continuity, and asks who maintains it, and at what cost.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Tradition gives a person a place in a sequence that began before him and will continue after, which softens the thought of ending. Zapffe's anchors work by supplying firm points in the flow, and a lineage is one of the oldest. The piety it asks is often repaid in a sense of being known.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — The Shattered God: the scattered world that the tradition gathers up. XV — The Last Messiah: the end of the line, which the lineage keeps out of sight.

description.p: A fixed thought or routine is used to get through sleeplessness.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The Insomniac sees clearly in the night. Anchoring moves the same hours onto something fixed, so that waking thought is already occupied: a prayer, a ledger, a task for tomorrow. Lucidity then runs along a prepared track and reaches only the points that the track allows.

section.label: Image
section.p: A woman sits up in bed at night with a rosary, or a ring of keys, in her hand, and a list is pinned to the wall by the lamp. Beyond the window the sky is dark and without stars. Her face is calm, and the shadow of the bedpost falls across the page like a bar.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the holding-fast used against the small hours.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A fixed thought or routine is used to get through sleeplessness. The card describes the means a person has found to keep from the open question, and whether they have been enough.

section.label: Defence
section.p: The small hours are hard, and a settled practice is a decent defence against them. Zapffe does not treat the damping of consciousness as a failing, since without it most people could not sleep, work or care for anyone. Nothing in the card suggests that the prayer or the list should be given up.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — The Insomniac: the lucidity the fixed thought keeps within bounds. XI — The Stone: a way of continuing that does not claim to settle the question.

description.p: Security rests on someone else's arrangements.

section.label: Age
section.p: Childhood. Hartmann assigned the first illusion, happiness in the present life, to the child. The anchors at this age are chosen by other people: parents, home, the school, the faith of the household. The child has no need to hold them in place, because the surrounding adults do it, and the world appears as it is told.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A small child holds the hand of an adult who is larger than the frame, in the manner of Goya's drawings of children. The child looks up and not ahead. Behind the pair a gate stands open on a road that neither of them looks at.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the anchor given before it could be chosen.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Security rests on someone else's arrangements. The card describes a person who holds to what was handed over in childhood, and who may not yet know it as a choice.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A child needs fixed points before it can understand why it needs them, and the loss of them in early years is among the hardest things to repair. Zapffe's mechanisms are mostly adopted without reflection, and the child has the best claim to this.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: Hartmann's stage of childhood. III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the faith that is passed down with the household.

description.p: A person has found something to give himself to and gives it everything.

section.label: Age
section.p: Youth. Hartmann tied the second illusion, happiness hereafter, to this age, when a person goes looking for something to give himself to. The young adopt an anchor with enthusiasm: a creed, a movement, a vocation, a person. The commitment is often total, because there is not yet anything else to weigh it against.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A young man stands before a crowd with a flag in his hands, or a young woman at the door of a seminary, in either case with a bag packed at their feet. Their gaze is fixed on the horizon, and the light falls on the face. Behind them the road they have left runs back to a small house.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the anchor chosen for the first time and held with conviction.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A person has found something to give himself to and gives it everything. The card marks the strength of the first commitment, and the quiet that comes if it turns out to be one of several.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Conviction gives the young a direction and a community at the moment they most need both. Many lasting works and friendships begin in a zeal that later looks excessive. The hardest to bear would be a youth without anything to believe in.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: Hartmann's stage of youth. IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the cause that the young often take up next.

description.p: Commitments are many and the days are full.

section.label: Age
section.p: Adulthood. Hartmann assigned the third illusion, progress, to this age, and it is the age at which anchors are many: a career, a household, a mortgage, a standing in the community. Schopenhauer's essay on the periods of life treats the middle years as the time of practical engagement, and the load of obligation protects against reflection.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A man in the middle years carries a child on one shoulder and a satchel on the other, in the manner of an etching of a market town. He is walking fast, and the streets are crowded around him. On the wall behind, the posted notices and tax rolls are numerous.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the many anchors of full adult life and the obligations that come with them.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Commitments are many and the days are full. The card describes a person who is held by duties on every side, and who has little occasion to ask where the duties lead.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Responsibility for other people is among the most dependable sources of meaning, and it is largely carried out by adults in their middle years. Zapffe names the family and the career among the anchors because they are at once the commonest and the most useful. The world is kept running by people too occupied to doubt it.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: Hartmann's stage of adulthood. V — Vanity: the question that the full days leave unasked.

description.p: The fixed points of a life are fewer, and the ones left are held with care.

section.label: Age
section.p: Old age, which Hartmann's three illusions leave out. The anchors of the earlier ages begin to loosen: the career ends, the children leave and friends die. Some elders return to the faith of childhood or hold more tightly to the family and the home. Others find that the supports have given way, and this is the age at which the mechanism is tested.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old woman sits in a doorway with a worn prayer book, or a bundle of letters, in her lap, in the manner of Goya's late drawings of the aged. A younger person stands beside her with a hand on the chair. The chair is anchored to the wall with a chain of old keys.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the anchors that remain, and those that have been lost.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The fixed points of a life are fewer, and the ones left are held with care. The card asks what has been kept, what has been put down, and what steadies a person at the end.

section.label: Defence
section.p: The last years are often easier for those with a faith, a family or a place to which they are tied. Zapffe's mechanisms are no less needed at the end than at the beginning. An old person who holds to a few things firmly has made a sound use of what remains.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — The Last Messiah: the end toward which the anchors, in the end, all point. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: the calm that comes when the anchors are loosened and not replaced.

description.p: Every spare minute has been given a task, and none is left for thought.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The excess of consciousness in card I is held off by never leaving it idle. A radio runs while the dishes are washed, a podcast while the dog is walked, a screen until the light goes out. Each gap in the day is filled before the mind can turn to what it sees.

section.label: Image
section.p: A woman sits at a kitchen table at night, lit from below by a small bright rectangle in her hands. On the wall behind her hangs a hunting trophy of enormous antlers, its shadow spread across the ceiling. She does not look up.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the habit of continuous input and the unease it covers.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Every spare minute has been given a task, and none is left for thought.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Zapffe's starting point is that a mind with spare capacity turns it on its own situation, and panic follows. A steady supply of small impressions is the cheapest remedy. It asks for no belief, and it lets a person work and look after others despite an awareness that would otherwise get in the way.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — The Giant Deer: the excess that the distraction occupies. X — The Insomniac: the night, when the supply runs thin.

description.p: The next treat is always already chosen.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card II holds that satisfaction in the present does not last. Distraction keeps the question from being asked by supplying the next pleasure before the last has faded: the purchase, the outing, the plans for the weekend.

section.label: Image
section.p: An arcade of lit shop windows at dusk. A woman with parcels on both arms stops at the next window, and behind her a parcel lies open on the pavement, its contents half out of the paper and forgotten.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names pleasure used to keep attention moving.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The next treat is always already chosen. Much of the enjoyment lies in anticipation, and the thing itself is soon put aside.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Pleasures are real, and a day of small ones is better than a day without. A person who is looking forward to something is spared the larger view for the time being, and for many people the rhythm of wanting and getting is the plainest form of ordinary cheer.
