section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the hope that the next pleasure will be the lasting one. VI — The Pendulum: the pause between purchases, which the arrangement avoids.

description.p: Busy service has taken the place of the question it was meant to answer.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card III places happiness after death, and a parish can hold the question of its truth at a distance through activity: rotas, bazaars, committees, repairs to the roof. The hereafter is so thoroughly arranged for that no one has leisure to ask whether it is there.

section.label: Image
section.p: A church hall after the service, with trestle tables and cake stalls. Women count coins into a tin, and a man on a ladder hangs a banner. Through the open door a priest stands alone in the nave, looking at the altar.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names a belief kept in motion by the work of maintaining it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Busy service has taken the place of the question it was meant to answer. The card asks what the hurry protects.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A congregation's activity does real good, in food, company and care for the sick. What lies beyond death is among the questions a mind cannot settle, and a community that sets it aside for shared work has chosen sensibly.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the hope that the activity surrounds. XII — Compassion: the part of the work that needs no belief to justify it.

description.p: Attention is held by what is new, and the present is a waiting room.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card IV places happiness in the future of the world. News, launches, updates and forecasts keep attention fixed on what comes next, and each novelty is received as a step on the road. Where the road leads is not asked, since the next announcement has arrived.

section.label: Image
section.p: A crowd waits in the dark outside a shuttered shop, wrapped in coats, some on folding chairs. Inside, a clerk sets a single object on a pedestal under a lamp. A clock in the square stands at midnight.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names novelty as a way of living in the future.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Attention is held by what is new, and the present is a waiting room. The card asks whether the thing awaited has ever, on arrival, been enough.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Curiosity about new things is a source of energy, and some novelties do improve life. Zapffe's concern is with a consciousness that has nothing to occupy it, and a flow of new matter is among the most dependable occupations.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the faith in the future that the stream of novelty feeds. V — Vanity: the Preacher's remark that nothing is new under the sun.

description.p: The workload has grown until it leaves no room to ask whether the work is worth doing.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card V finds labour without lasting profit. Distraction answers by multiplying the labour: the full diary, the overflowing inbox, tasks that generate further tasks. Being busy is taken as evidence that the work matters, and the afternoon on which its worth might be asked never comes.

section.label: Image
section.p: A clerk sits at a desk heaped with papers that spill on to the floor and climb the walls, while a boy carries in another pile. On the sill, half hidden by a ledger, stands a small hourglass.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names busyness as protection against the question of purpose.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The workload has grown until it leaves no room to ask whether the work is worth doing.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Work provides income, structure and a sense of being needed, and an occupied person is useful to others. Zapffe treats such absorption as one of the ways a mind stays functional. Even the Preacher, who calls labour vanity, advises enjoying its fruit.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Vanity: the futility that the pile covers. XI — The Stone: labour taken up without the excuse of being busy.

description.p: Boredom is avoided before it can be felt.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card VI describes the swing between want and boredom. Distraction shortens the second phase: at the first sign of an empty moment the hand goes to the phone, the radio, the cupboard. The pendulum turns so quickly that the lower end is hardly reached.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man in a railway waiting room reads a newspaper, glances at his watch, folds the paper, takes out another and unfolds it. A pendulum clock swings behind glass over his head, and the travellers on the benches do much the same.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the quick filling of every idle moment.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Boredom is avoided before it can be felt. The card asks what happens in the moment before the hand moves.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Boredom is unpleasant, and for a person with no means of bearing it can be worse. A ready supply of small occupations spares everyone the worst of it. A mind that stops may stop at something it cannot face, and Zapffe counts the capacity to keep moving as a sign of health.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — The Pendulum: the swing whose slow end the card shortens. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: a pause taken in attention instead of being filled.

description.p: The surroundings are enjoyed at a distance that keeps them safe.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card VII shows an indifferent nature that does not listen. Distraction keeps this at the edge of attention by turning nature into scenery or programme: the weather forecast, the documentary with its narrating voice, the resort with its loudspeaker. The storm becomes an item.

section.label: Image
section.p: A family sits on a crowded beach under a striped awning, a radio playing, children shrieking at a ball. On the horizon a bank of black cloud rises over the water. Only the lifeguard, on his high chair, has turned to look.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names nature as entertainment, with the indifference left out.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The surroundings are enjoyed at a distance that keeps them safe. Met without the screen, they would speak less pleasantly.

section.label: Defence
section.p: The beach is a pleasure and the forecast is useful. Attending to the pleasant surface of the world is a condition of ordinary life, and a family that spent the afternoon contemplating the cosmos would have had no afternoon.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — Nature and the Icelander: the indifferent world that the radio is turned up against. IX — The Shattered God: the account that gives the indifference an origin.

description.p: Conversation has become a way of not being alone with anyone.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card VIII describes the right distance between people. Distraction keeps a distance without having to find one, by surrounding every meeting with activity: the party, the group message, the television left on during dinner. People are together, and nobody has to come near.

section.label: Image
section.p: A long table crowded with guests, every mouth open and every glass raised, each turned half toward a neighbour and half toward the next sound. At the far end two porcupines sit still on the tablecloth, eating from the same dish.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names company used as noise.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Conversation has become a way of not being alone with anyone. The evenings are full, and something is missing from them.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Sociability is a pleasure and a duty, and shared noise is a kind of warmth. Schopenhauer's parable grants that the cold drives people together. The party spares each guest the harder task of attending to the others, and often to himself.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Porcupines: the distance that the crowd lets people avoid settling. XII — Compassion: attention paid to one person, which the noise prevents.

description.p: Attention is occupied with details that do not add up to a picture.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card IX shows a world made of the fragments of something finished. Distraction supplies fragments in quantity and lets attention move among them: the collection, the feed, the puzzle, the hobby with its endless small parts. The whole is never asked for.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man sits at a long workbench sorting broken china into shallow trays by colour and size. Trays cover every surface. On the wall behind him hangs an empty frame.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names the sorting of small things as a way of not seeing the whole.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Attention is occupied with details that do not add up to a picture. The card asks what the picture was supposed to be.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Collecting and puzzling are among the oldest pleasures and often the most absorbing. They give hands and eyes a task that can be finished, which the larger questions rarely do. The sorter has found, in a shattered world, a scale on which it is possible to live.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — The Shattered God: the broken whole whose pieces the card handles. XIII — The Broom: a different way of living among remains, which accepts them.

description.p: The nights are filled so that the mind has no chance to turn to itself.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Card X is the mind awake at night with nothing to do but see. Distraction fills the dark as it fills the day: the television left on, the radio under the pillow, the screen held above the face. Lucidity is met with a murmur of other people's voices.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man lies in bed in a small room, lit by the blue flicker of a screen, his eyes open. Across the street another window glows blue, and beyond it a row of others.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names noise used against sleeplessness and its thoughts.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The nights are filled so that the mind has no chance to turn to itself. The screen makes the night easier and leaves the cause of the wakefulness where it was.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Sleep matters, and a person who has lain awake for hours is entitled to whatever helps. Zapffe never asked anyone to meet his thoughts unaided at three in the morning. A voice on the radio keeps a lonely hour company.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — The Insomniac: the lucidity that the noise is set against. VI — The Pendulum: the boredom of the long night.

description.p: An absorption that has not yet become a defence.

section.label: Age
section.p: Schopenhauer describes childhood as a time when the world is seen with fresh eyes and the child is occupied almost wholly by what it perceives. Attention goes where colour, sound or movement is, and moves on, so that nothing is held long enough to oppress.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A child of about five sits on a nursery floor among toys and picture-books, reaching for a coloured top while a drum lies half beaten beside it. Through the window the garden stands in rain, unnoticed.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names attention held without effort by a supply of new things.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: An absorption that has not yet become a defence.

section.label: Defence
section.p: For a child distraction is a method of growth. The mind has not yet acquired the excess that Zapffe describes, and play is how it learns the world. Turning a child from a grief to a toy is a kindness that usually works.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — The First Illusion: Happiness Here: the stage Hartmann assigns to childhood. 0 — The Unborn: the condition before awareness has anything to damp.

description.p: A time of restless movement among attractions, each held lightly.

section.label: Age
section.p: Schopenhauer describes youth as a restless age, full of longing, in which the future seems to promise more than it will give. Distraction takes the form of constant stimulation: music, parties, fashion, rivalry, the next person met.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A young man in an evening coat stands in the doorway of a ballroom, one foot on the stair to a second room where music is playing, his head turned toward a third. Behind him masked dancers cross the floor in lines.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names appetite for experience used to keep quiet questions away.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A time of restless movement among attractions, each held lightly. It may also describe a person of any age who keeps the pace of youth because slowing down would raise questions.

section.label: Defence
section.p: The energy of youth needs somewhere to go, and variety of experience is how it finds a place. Dancing is a good use of an evening.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter: the hope Hartmann ties to youth, kept alive by motion. VI — The Pendulum: the swing that the pace is meant to hide.

description.p: A life managed efficiently, with little left over.

section.label: Age
section.p: Hartmann ties adulthood to the hope of progress, and Schopenhauer treats the middle years as the age of plans and duties. Distraction takes the form of scheduling. The diary, the commute and the household tasks use up the hours and leave no room to ask what they add up to.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A man in his forties in a plain dark coat crosses a station concourse at speed, a briefcase in one hand and a telephone at his ear, a child's coat over his arm. A crowd flows around him in both directions.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names obligation used to fill the hours.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A life managed efficiently, with little left over. The card asks whether the demands are all real, or whether some are sought so that something else can be left unexamined.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Most of the obligations are real. Children need feeding and bills need paying, and the busy adult is doing what his position requires. Responsibility serves others as well as the self.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — The Third Illusion: Progress: the hope of a better future that the plans serve. V — Vanity: the afternoon on which the plans are looked at.

description.p: Attention held by small and regular matters.

section.label: Age
section.p: Hartmann's three illusions leave out old age. Schopenhauer remarks that in later years life offers less that is new, and the strength to pursue it declines. Distraction narrows to small things: the crossword, the television, the garden, the post, meals at fixed hours.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old woman sits in an armchair by a window, a knitting basket on her knee and a wireless on the shelf beside her. A newspaper lies folded on the sill with a crossword half done. She watches a blackbird on the lawn in the lamplight of a late afternoon.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The card names routine as a quiet form of distraction.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Attention held by small and regular matters.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Habit is a mercy in old age. The rhythm of meals, post and programmes gives each day a form that takes no strength to make. An old person who lives gently on small impressions is managing well.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — The Pendulum: the swing that routine slows to a gentle sway. XIV — The Stilled Wheel: the calm that routine can approach without reaching.

description.p: An excess of awareness has found something to hold.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The excess of consciousness is given a use. A draughtsman studies the antlers of an extinct deer, and the surplus that Zapffe saw as a biological error becomes attention, patience and a finished drawing. The overgrowth is accepted as a fact and put to work.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure at a table in a museum store-room, drawing a vast antler from a skull set on a trestle. The paper on the board is already crowded with fine hatching, and the drawn antler is slightly larger than the real one. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The first use of a faculty that has outgrown its purpose. The card names the moment when too much mind finds an object worth its weight.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: An excess of awareness has found something to hold. The matter is not resolved, but it has acquired a shape. The card asks what the surplus is currently making.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Zapffe held that a consciousness too large for survival must be damped or it becomes unbearable, and he treated sublimation as the rarest of the four mechanisms and the only one that damps by transforming. Pain that becomes a drawing is neither denied nor buried, and the maker keeps sight of the cause. He also thought the mechanism rare, since few people have the gift or the leisure. Whether it works for the maker or only for the audience he left open.

section.label: Links
section.p: I, The Giant Deer: the same overgrowth, here put to use. XIV, The Stilled Wheel: contemplation of a form, which rests the will for a time.

description.p: Joy is being turned into something that outlasts it.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The hope of happiness in this life is given form in a still life or a love poem. The brief pleasure, which the card admits will not last, is painted at the height of its ripeness, so that it can be looked at without being owned. The loss is built into the picture.

section.label: Image
section.p: A painter at an easel before a table set with peaches, a half-peeled lemon and a glass. One peach has begun to soften, and the painter has put it at the centre of the canvas. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Happiness here, kept as a record. The card names the pleasure that is enjoyed and then recorded as a form, with its transience visible.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Joy is being turned into something that outlasts it. The pleasure is real and so is its end, and the card allows both. It suggests making a record of what is good now.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A person who writes down a happy day does not expect it to return. The record lets the day count without the claim that it was permanent. Zapffe would grant that this costs little and gives much. He also noted how seldom the mechanism is open to people, since it needs a talent or a craft, and he would ask whether the painter is happier or only more occupied.

section.label: Links
section.p: II, The First Illusion: Happiness Here, which the still life holds without believing in it. V, Vanity: the genre of vanitas painting, in which pleasure and its end share a canvas.

description.p: Longing has been turned into craft.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The hope of happiness hereafter is given form as music. A choir rehearses a mass in an unheated church, and the promise of another world becomes a sound that exists in this one. The afterlife is not believed, but the longing behind it is allowed to shape something.

section.label: Image
section.p: A small choir in a stone nave, singing from a single shared score under one lamp. Above them the vault is dark and empty, and the singers look up at it without seeing anything. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The longing for a world beyond, made into a work. The card names what remains of religious feeling when the doctrine has gone.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Longing has been turned into craft. The hope of a hereafter is no longer asked to be true, and it is still allowed to be beautiful. The card points to the work that the longing can produce.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Hartmann argued that the second illusion fails, and Zapffe offered no replacement. Sublimation supplies one that asks for no belief. A hymn sung by someone who doubts it still steadies him, and the tradition that built it kept many people going through hard years. Zapffe would add that this is a gift to a few, and that the rest need a firmer anchor.

section.label: Links
section.p: III, The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter, here emptied of doctrine and kept as music. XIV, The Stilled Wheel: the will quiet for the length of a piece.

description.p: Work is justified by the task and not by the outcome.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The illusion of progress is given form as a monument to the work of earlier generations. A restorer repairs a fresco knowing that the wall will outlast her and that nothing will be finished. The truth that the future will not redeem the past is accepted, and the effort is spent on the thing in front of her.

section.label: Image
section.p: A scaffold against a cracked wall in a half-ruined chapel, where a restorer in a smock fills in a missing patch of sky with a fine brush. Beside her a bucket of lime and a ladder. Sections of the fresco beyond her reach are already flaking. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Work done without a promise of improvement. The card names effort that does not depend on history arriving anywhere.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Work is justified by the task and not by the outcome. The expected progress has not arrived, and the work remains worth doing. The card advises attending to the piece at hand.

section.label: Defence
section.p: The belief that history improves has sustained many labourers, and Hartmann treated its loss as the last disillusion. A craft offers a smaller and sturdier ground: the job is good when done well, whatever follows. Zapffe would remind us that the craftsman still needs to believe the work matters, which is an anchor of a kind, and that sublimation seldom stands alone.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV, The Third Illusion: Progress, replaced by care for a single task. XIII, The Broom: a plant that grows on ruined ground and asks for nothing.

description.p: An honest account of futility has itself become a task.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The vanity of labour under the sun, as Ecclesiastes states it, is given form in the preacher's own book. The writer sets down that all is breath, and the setting down is a labour that he does not exempt from the verdict. Form is the means by which he looks at the emptiness without being flattened by it.

section.label: Image
section.p: An old man at a plain desk, writing on a long roll of paper that falls over the edge and coils on the floor. A candle burns beside him and the shadow of the roll crosses the wall. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The statement of vanity as a work. The card names the writing that tells the truth about writing.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: An honest account of futility has itself become a task. The labour is acknowledged as breath, and it is carried out regardless. The card suggests that saying plainly what is the case is a use of the time.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Ecclesiastes has lasted longer than most books of comfort, which suggests that a clear statement of vanity can be consoling to a reader. Zapffe would accept this as an example of sublimation at its best, and he might add that the mechanism cannot be known to work from inside. His essay on the last messiah is itself a piece of writing, and he was aware that it might belong here.

section.label: Links
section.p: V, Vanity: the verdict that the book gives and does not escape. X, The Insomniac: a sleepless writer, who at least has something to do with the hours.

description.p: The restlessness has a form, and the form can be worked.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The swing between pain and boredom is given form as rhythm. A composer sets a restless period in a dull month to a metre, and the oscillation becomes a pattern with a beginning and an end. Pain and boredom are used as material instead of being fled.

section.label: Image
section.p: A woman at a pianoforte in a bare room, with a metronome beside the score. A pendulum shadow moves across the wall behind her, and the score is covered with corrections. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The oscillation as a measure. The card names the way that a recurring discomfort can be made into time that has a shape.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The restlessness has a form, and the form can be worked. Neither the pain nor the boredom has gone, but each now serves a pattern. The card suggests giving the swing a metre.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Schopenhauer wrote that aesthetic contemplation suspends the will for a time, and with it the swing. For an artist the periods of lull and torment are both useful, since one supplies material and the other leisure. Zapffe would observe that the swing resumes when the piece ends, and that the relief is therefore partial and renewable only by more work.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI, The Pendulum: the same swing, kept in time. XIV, The Stilled Wheel: the pause in the will that art affords.

description.p: The indifference of the world has become a subject of study.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Nature's indifference is given form as landscape. A painter sits before a cold shore and puts down what is there: the grey water, the empty sky, the absence of any sign that either regards him. The indifference becomes a subject, and a subject can be studied with care.

section.label: Image
section.p: A painter on a stony beach with a small folding stool, working at a panel in the wind. In front of him is a sea under a heavy sky, and a single small sail in the distance. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Indifference observed with attention. The card names the discipline of looking at a world that does not look back.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The indifference of the world has become a subject of study. Attention is repaid with detail, if not with comfort. The card suggests looking at the thing without asking it to answer.

section.label: Defence
section.p: In Leopardi's dialogue Nature answers the Icelander only that the world was not made for him, which leaves him with nothing but his own account. Sublimation lets that account be exact. Zapffe thought art was the one mechanism in which the cost of the knowledge is partly turned back into gain. He would also point out that most people cannot paint a shore, and that the sea is easier to bear for those who look at it for an afternoon than for those who are caught in a storm.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII, Nature and the Icelander: the silence of nature, here recorded faithfully. XIII, The Broom: Leopardi's own poem, which belongs to this kind of work.

description.p: Distance has been made into a medium.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: The problem of the right distance between people is given form as correspondence. Two friends write long letters over many years, and the page supplies the space that sitting together lacks. Warmth is exchanged without the pricks of proximity.

section.label: Image
section.p: Two desks in two rooms of different towns, each with a lamp and a sheet half written. A road drawn faintly through the window of each connects them. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Closeness at a workable distance. The card names the forms, such as letters, art and books, through which people reach one another without crowding.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Distance has been made into a medium. The relationship can be warm because it is mediated, and the card suggests that a form may carry what direct contact cannot. It invites writing rather than visiting.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Schopenhauer's porcupines found a tolerable distance by trial and wound. A letter or a poem is a distance chosen in advance, and many friendships have survived because of one. Zapffe would grant its value and add that he expected few to practise it, since it demands skill and time. The reader of a book is also a partner who cannot answer, which is part of its comfort.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII, The Porcupines: the right distance, found through form. XII, Compassion: warmth that can be given without contact.

description.p: The pieces have been arranged and not mended.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Mainländer's account of a God who shattered into the world is given form as a mosaic. A mason sets thousands of small pieces into a floor, and the whole is made of fragments that remain visibly separate. The picture does not restore the unity and does not conceal the breaks.

section.label: Image
section.p: A mason kneeling on a floor, setting small tesserae into a wide circular pattern with a trowel. Most of the circle is complete and a few gaps remain, with a heap of loose stone beside him. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Fragmentation made orderly. The card names the arrangement of broken things into a pattern that is not a repair.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The pieces have been arranged and not mended. The fragmentation is acknowledged, and a design has been found within it. The card suggests that a coherent whole can be made from parts that were never one.

section.label: Defence
section.p: If everything is a fragment of a lost unity, any arrangement of fragments is a kind of orientation. A mosaic gives the viewer a fixed point without a false claim about the origin. Zapffe would see this as the productive form of anchoring, and would note that the mason must keep his eyes on the stones to be content, and the same can be said of anyone who works.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX, The Shattered God: the fragments of Mainländer's metaphysics, set in order. XIV, The Stilled Wheel: the quiet that follows when the pattern is complete.

description.p: Sleeplessness has become productive.

section.label: Evasion
section.p: Lucidity without rest is given form as the night's work. The insomniac does not sleep, and uses the hours to write. Cioran described a life of sleepless nights and wrote a great deal during them, and the card follows that pattern without claiming it as a cure. The wakefulness yields pages.

section.label: Image
section.p: A narrow room at night with a single window, through which a pale sky shows. A man sits at a desk with a pen, and a neat stack of finished pages stands at his elbow. The bed behind him is made. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Wakefulness used. The card names the transformation of a sleepless mind into a body of work.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Sleeplessness has become productive. The mind is not at rest, and its restlessness now has an outlet. The card suggests that a long night can be given a task.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Cioran's lucidity could be a torment, and the pages he wrote were a way of living with it. Zapffe regarded this as the most dignified response he knew, and the least common. He doubted it could be recommended, because the gift is not given to all, and because writing about wakefulness may deepen it. He allowed that the result might be worth the price.

section.label: Links
section.p: X, The Insomniac: the same lucidity, spent on work. XI, The Stone: a labour repeated each day without hope of an end.

description.p: Making is still free of purpose.

section.label: Age
section.p: Childhood in Schopenhauer's account is a time when the world is taken in through the senses and has the freshness of the new, and when play is the chief activity. Sublimation here is play: a drawing, a song, a story told to a toy. Hartmann tied the first illusion to childhood, and the child's art is made inside it, with no thought of consolation.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A child sitting on a floor, drawing on a large sheet with a stub of chalk. The drawing shows a house, a sun and a very large animal with antlers. Nobody is watching. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Making before there is anything to make against. The card names the play from which later art grows.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Making is still free of purpose. The activity is its own reward, and nothing has yet been asked of it. The card points to what the maker did before the work had to justify itself.

section.label: Defence
section.p: A child's drawing protects nothing in particular, since the child has not yet met the thing it might protect against. That is its value: the habit of making is acquired early and is available later, when the need arises. Zapffe saw sublimation as rare, and the capacity may be best preserved by those who are allowed to play. Children also stop drawing at a certain age, as most adults notice.

section.label: Links
section.p: II, The First Illusion: Happiness Here, in its earliest and least troubled form. I, The Giant Deer: a mind with room to grow, using it for pictures.

description.p: Strong feeling is looking for a form.

section.label: Age
section.p: Schopenhauer described youth as a period of ardent expectation, and Hartmann tied the second illusion to it. In this suit the feeling of youth, its yearning and its dissatisfaction, is written into verse, music or a first novel. The excess of feeling finds a form because it has nowhere else to go.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A young person in an attic room, writing by lamplight, with loose pages on the floor and a violin on the bed. The window is open, and a town lies below it. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Longing made into work. The card names the apprentice years, in which feeling is large and technique is small.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Strong feeling is looking for a form. The results may be imperfect, and the effort is the point. The card suggests that the intensity of the present is raw material.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Much of the world's art was written by the young, and for many the habit of writing carried them past years that might have gone worse. The mechanism protects them from their own intensity. Zapffe's reservation applies: the great majority of the young who write poems do not become poets, and some come to rely on the dream of fame, which is a different anchor. Still, the poem is written.

section.label: Links
section.p: III, The Second Illusion: Happiness Hereafter, the yearning for something beyond, given an earthly outlet. VI, The Pendulum: the swings of youthful mood, set to rhythm.

description.p: A regular practice is giving structure to a difficult period.

section.label: Age
section.p: Schopenhauer's middle years bring responsibility, repetition and a measured view of what is possible. Hartmann tied the third illusion, progress, to adulthood. Sublimation in this age is craft: a trade, a body of work built up in the evenings, a practice kept up beside other duties. The pain of adult life is turned into steady output.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A middle-aged woman at a workbench after the day's labour, carving a small figure from wood. A coat hangs on a nail, supper dishes stand on a shelf, and shavings lie on the floor. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Craft sustained beside duty. The card names the art that grows in the margin of an ordinary life.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A regular practice is giving structure to a difficult period. It is modest and it holds. The card suggests protecting the hour set aside for it.

section.label: Defence
section.p: For an adult with obligations, the sustained practice is one of the few forms of sublimation available, and it is cheaper than a grand project. Zapffe rated the mechanism rare, and Schopenhauer thought that most people live without such an interest. Work done in the evening may be of modest worth to others and of great worth to the person doing it, which is enough for the card.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV, The Third Illusion: Progress, replaced by the slow accumulation of work. V, Vanity: labour under the sun, here with a visible product.

description.p: A long experience has reached the stage of being passed on.

section.label: Age
section.p: Schopenhauer saw old age as a time of calm, in which the passions have lessened and the mind turns more freely to what is lasting. Hartmann's three illusions leave out this age. Sublimation here is the late work: a memoir, a final cycle of drawings, a garden laid out for others. The long view is put into a form for those who come later.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old man sitting in a garden, with a sketchbook on his knee. A young apprentice stands at his shoulder, holding a roll of paper, and the old man is pointing to a place on the page. No text appears in the image.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The late work and its handing on. The card names the form given to a lifetime's understanding.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A long experience has reached the stage of being passed on. The pace is unhurried and the form is settled. The card suggests that what has been learned is ready to be made into something another person can use.

section.label: Defence
section.p: Late work is often the plainest, and it is made when ambition has fallen away and the maker has little to defend. It protects the elder from the sense that a life has left nothing behind. Zapffe doubted that humanity as a whole would use its gift well, and he would see the elder as an exception. He would also ask who inherits the work, and whether it is read.

section.label: Links
section.p: XIV, The Stilled Wheel: the quiet of age, spent on contemplation. XIII, The Broom: a gift made for others on poor ground.
